summary: Describes a YANG library giving information about YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas used by a network management server, with simple caching so clients can avoid re-reading it. It supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8525 defines a YANG Library that tells clients which data models and schemas a network-management server supports. A content identifier lets clients cache that information and detect when it changes.

questions: how to list yang modules on a server
what is a yang module set
subtitle: How a management server describes its YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas.

tldr.problem: A management client needs to know which YANG modules and schemas a server uses in each datastore. The earlier library format assumed all datastores shared the same schema.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-yang-library module lists module sets, schemas made from those sets, datastores that use each schema, and a content identifier that changes when the library changes.
tldr.outcome: Clients can cache the library and check its identifier before retrieving it again. RFC 8525 obsoletes RFC 7895 and is updated by RFC 10035.

today: RFC 8525 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7895 and is updated by RFC 10035.

sections.title: Why a YANG Library Is Needed
sections.content:
A network-management client needs to know which YANG modules, datastores and datastore schemas a server supports. RFC 8525 defines the ietf-yang-library module to provide that information.

The previous library format assumed that every datastore had the same schema. The Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) allows a dynamic configuration datastore to have its own schema, and the operational state datastore may include modules that are not configurable. The library can differ between servers and may change at runtime or after a restart.
sections.plainLanguage: The client needs a current description of the models and schemas a server supports. Separate datastores may use different schemas, so the library describes them individually.

sections.title: Information Clients Need
sections.content:
For each YANG module, clients need its name, revision, submodules, supported features and any deviation modules that affect it. For each datastore, clients need its identity and the schema it uses.

The design allows a dynamic configuration datastore to implement a module or feature not used by conventional configuration datastores. It also allows an operational datastore to omit modules implemented elsewhere. A given module uses one revision across the datastores in which it is implemented, while import-only uses may refer to revisions as needed. The library is designed to work with schema mount.
sections.plainLanguage: The library identifies each model and the features the server supports. It also connects each datastore to the schema that describes its data.

sections.title: Module Sets, Schemas and Datastores
sections.content:
The /yang-library container holds module sets, schemas, datastores and a content identifier. A module set is a named collection of modules and submodules; it also describes features and deviations. Import-only modules list definitions that the server uses but does not implement as accessible data.

A schema is the union of one or more module sets. Each datastore entry points to its schema. Multiple datastores can share a schema, and the operational schema can be a superset of the schemas used for conventional configuration. The library data nodes are config false, so they are available in operational state.

The earlier /modules-state tree and related definitions remain for backward compatibility but are deprecated. NMDA-aware clients use /yang-library; legacy clients can continue using the older tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Module sets group related models, schemas combine module sets, and each datastore points to a schema. The older library data remains available as deprecated information for compatibility.

sections.title: Caching with the Content Identifier
sections.content:
The content-id is a server-generated identifier for the current library information. Its value must change whenever that information changes; the same library content does not have to produce the same identifier every time.

A client can fetch the library once, cache it, and retrieve it again only after noticing a new identifier. When the identifier changes, the server also generates a yang-library-update notification. A NETCONF server supporting the NMDA extensions may also update its advertised capability and send a capability-change notification as specified by the relevant NETCONF documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The content identifier is a change marker for the library. Clients can compare it with the value they cached and fetch new details only when the marker changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG Library is intended to be read through network-management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, using secure transport. Access-control rules can restrict which users can read its contents.

The list of modules, revisions, features and deviations may reveal details about the server and help an attacker identify known weaknesses. The RFC therefore says that operators should control read access to these data nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The library can reveal which software capabilities a server has. Operators should limit access to it when that information is sensitive.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC takes over the XML namespace registration previously associated with RFC 7895 and changes its registrant contact to the IESG. It also registers the YANG module name ietf-yang-library, its namespace and the prefix yanglib in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA records the module's namespace and name so that implementations can refer to the same YANG Library consistently.
